— 🇺🇸/🇮🇷 What was Iran's reaction to the September 11 attacks?
The morning following 9/11, thousands of Iranians gathered in the streets of the capital Tehran to hold a candlelight vigil for the victims. According to eyewitnesses, the vigil lasted for several miles.
At Tehran's largest soccer stadium, a crowd of 60,000 people observed a minute of silence and recited prayers for those killed, before the start of Iran's World Cup qualification match.
On the same day, the Iranian President at the time, Mohammad Khatami, said the following: 'On behalf of the Iranian people and the Islamic Republic of Iran, I denounce this terrorist act, which led to the killing of defenseless people, and I express my deepest sorrow and sympathy with the American people.'
The Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, also commented on the attack: 'Islam condemns the massacre of defenseless people, whether Muslim or Christian or others, anywhere and by any means. However, this act should not be used as a pretext to carry out any attack on Afghanistan, which will lead to another human tragedy.'

An Israeli official told Channel 12 that Houthi control of Bab-el-Mandeb is more dangerous than the current Hormuz situation, and the reason is simple geometry. 
The eastern shipping channel past Perim Island is only about 3 km wide. 
Ships will pass within visual range of Houthi positions. 
Israeli official:
They will be able to fire at whatever they want with anti-tank missiles. 
They will be able to see the ships with their own eyes.
That's the difference. 
At Hormuz, Iran needs radar, surveillance systems, and anti-ship missiles to threaten traffic. 
At Bab-el-Mandeb, a fighter with a basic ATGM on Perim Island can hit a tanker he can physically see. 
No sophisticated targeting required. The official said this gives the Houthis "enormous power."

events.text:
Videos show the scale of equipment the Houthis captured during the western coast offensive. 
The "booty" footage from Mokha and surrounding positions includes U.S.-made Oshkosh M-ATV mine-resistant vehicles, pickup trucks mounted with heavy weapons (technicals), armored vehicles, artillery pieces, and large quantities of ammunition and small arms abandoned by retreating National Resistance and Giants Brigade forces.
Houthi fighters are filming themselves inspecting, posing with, and driving captured vehicles around Mokha's port and airport. 
Some clips show rows of intact military vehicles left behind, suggesting parts of the retreat were disorganized enough that equipment wasn't destroyed or disabled before withdrawal.
The captured gear originally came from Saudi Arabia and the UAE, who supplied their Yemeni proxy forces over years of fighting.

events.title: Telegram
events.text:
Yemen’s Houthis say they launched a large-scale military operation on September 3 against Saudi-backed forces on Yemen’s western coast, citing continued attacks, military buildups, and the blockade imposed on the country.
The group said the operation was carried out from several directions with support from local tribes.
According to the Houthis, the operation resulted in the capture of six districts in Taiz and Hodeidah governorates, covering around 5,400 square kilometers.
They also said seven military divisions, including 38 brigades, were targeted, with hundreds of fighters killed, wounded, or captured.
The Houthis said a number of their prisoners held on the western coast were also freed.
They added that their air defenses carried out 32 interception operations and shot down nine Saudi aircraft.
The Houthis also said maritime navigation remains safe for all companies except Saudi vessels, which they said remain subject to blockade.
They reiterated their policy of “a siege for a siege” and said attacks on Saudi military positions would continue until the fighting stops and the blockade on Yemen is lifted.

⚡️🇺🇸🇾🇪 Anthropic says Yemen-based actors (most likely Ansar-Allah) used Claude to develop guided weapons
Anthropic says it identified a group of threat actors in northern Yemen that used Claude Code to develop software for guided weapons, including a guided rocket, a ballistic missile programme and a missile variant involving a hypersonic glide vehicle.
The company said the actors used multiple Claude instances for coding, research and code review, while attempting to evade safeguards by hiding their goals and splitting work across sessions.
Anthropic said its safeguards blocked many requests, but not all. The group eventually test-fired a guided rocket, which appears to have failed, and returned to Claude to investigate the failure.

🇾🇪👤 Yemeni weapons cell used Anthropic's Claude to build missile software — report
A weapons engineering cell in Yemen used Anthropic's Claude models to create guidance and control software for rockets and missiles, a new report from Anthropic titled "Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026" shows.
👉 The cell was juggling three weapons programs at once: a guided rocket with final-phase homing, a multi-stage ballistic missile aiming for a range beyond 2,000 km, and something called the "R2000" — which included a hypersonic glide vehicle variant.
Instead of hiring a team of software engineers, they leaned on Claude Code as their entire development layer. They ran several instances of Claude side by side, each with a different job — one writing code, one doing technical research, one checking the others' work.
➡️ Anthropic's filters blocked plenty of their direct requests. So the operators got creative: they hid what the work was actually for, split their prompts across isolated sessions so no single log showed the full picture, and used other workarounds to stay under the radar.
Anthropic says there is no evidence the group succeeded in fielding a working long-range weapon. That said, the cell did test-fire a guided rocket — and the test appears to have failed. Within hours, they were back in Claude running a failure analysis on the telemetry.
Once Anthropic caught on, it banned the accounts and shared what it found with security partners in both the public and private sectors. But by then, the group had already compiled some offline simulation tools — meaning they could keep working without Claude.

US builds $1.2M 'bunker-buster lab' after failing to crack Iran’s underground sites
 
The Pentagon is spending millions trying to solve a problem it has already struggled with: how to destroy Iran’s deeply buried nuclear infrastructure.
 
👉 Several days before the conflict with Iran began in late February, the Pentagon’s Defense Threat Reduction Agency published a document showing it had awarded almost a $1.2 million contract to upgrade a “unique subterranean test facility” at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico for a live-fire test aimed at developing capabilities against emerging underground threats.
 
Since early March, the remote location known as the Alternate Seismic Hardrock in Situ Test Site has continued to accumulate excavations, with the test site also carved into granite, similarly to Pickaxe Mountain.
 
➡️ Now, the US is reportedly preparing new tests at the simulated underground facility to develop methods for striking Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain site—a hardened underground complex near Natanz that Washington and Israel believe houses Iran’s enriched uranium stockpiles.
 
President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to target the site, arguing that hitting the underground facility would be necessary to limit Iran’s nuclear capabilities.
 
The challenge for the US is that even its largest conventional bunker-busting weapons may not guarantee the destruction of facilities built deep underground. Earlier strikes on facilities such as Natanz and Fordow were presented as major blows, yet Iran maintained the ability to preserve key underground infrastructure and continue operations.

🔥🇨🇳 China’s nuclear subs just got a missile built to reach the US
 
The Chinese navy is refitting its fleet of nuclear-powered submarines to carry the new JL-3 intercontinental ballistic missile, Taipei Times reports.
 
The JL-3 is expected to become a key pillar of China’s nuclear arsenal, strengthening the country’s ability to retaliate in the event of an enemy attack. 
 
Here’s why: 
 
🔴 The missile’s 10,000 km range allows China to target the northwestern US, as well as Alaska, Guam and Hawaii, from Chinese waters 
 
🔴 The JL-3 is capable of carrying multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicles, with at least three nuclear warheads per missile
 
🔴 An estimated yield of each warhead is around 250 to 1,000 kilotons, enabling a single missile to strike multiple targets
 
🔴 Unlike liquid-fuel missiles, the JL-3 uses solid fuel, making it easier to maintain aboard submarines while keeping it ready for launch
 
The JL-3 is therefore set to strengthen the sea-based leg of China's nuclear triad, giving the PLA a more survivable long-range strike capability from its submarine fleet.
